Treasury said the review was intended to improve payment integrity and had not delayed, stopped, or rerouted payments. patch.description_long: In early February 2025, the Treasury Department confirmed that a member of the government-efficiency team had read-only access to code associated with its federal payment system. Reuters reported that Treasury identified technology executive Tom Krause as leading the review and that the system handles more than $6 trillion in annual disbursements, including Social Security and Medicare payments. The review was presented by Treasury as an effort to improve payment integrity. The access prompted scrutiny because the payment infrastructure supports large federal programs and obligations to millions of recipients. Treasury said no payments had been suspended, rejected, delayed, or rerouted as a result of the review. Treasury described read-only access to payment-system code; it does not establish that DOGE had unrestricted authority to alter transactions, that the access lacked legal authorization, or that a breach or fraud occurred. The review prompted scrutiny of sensitive payment infrastructure even though Treasury said it had not interrupted or rerouted disbursements.

patch.description_long:
President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un met in Singapore on June 12, 2018, in the first summit between a sitting U.S. president and a North Korean leader. The meeting produced a joint statement in which the two governments pledged to pursue new U.S.–North Korea relations, work toward a lasting peace regime on the Korean Peninsula, and continue efforts toward the denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula. The statement also included a commitment to recover the remains of U.S. service members missing from the Korean War.

The summit was a highly visible diplomatic opening after years of hostility and threats, giving Kim direct engagement with a U.S. president. The text, however, used broad language and did not specify a denuclearization timetable, a verification process, or a detailed definition of the objective. The signed commitments were a framework for further diplomacy rather than a record of completed disarmament. For the United States, the document linked a new bilateral relationship to peace and denuclearization; for North Korea, it offered direct engagement at the presidential level. Implementing those commitments would require negotiations beyond the summit itself.

patch.description_long: On March 3, 2026, Israel-Hezbollah fighting widened as Israeli troops moved into southern Lebanon, Israeli airstrikes hit the country, and Hezbollah launched rockets toward Israel. The Associated Press reported that the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) had observed Israeli troops crossing the Blue Line into Lebanese territory at several locations and then returning. The reported crossings included areas near Markaba, Al Adeisse, and Kfar Kela. Israel’s military said its forces were operating in the area, while the AP account said it was unclear how many troops remained inside Lebanon. UNIFIL’s observations describe movements across the border; they do not by themselves establish a lasting occupation of each location. The fighting occurred alongside the U.S.-Iran confrontation, bringing another border into the wider regional conflict. AP’s account attributed the crossing observations to UNIFIL, while separately describing the Israeli military’s statements about its operations. Neither the reported crossings nor their timing established that President Donald Trump directed Israel’s movements.

patch.description_long: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s January 29, 2025 memorandum, “Restoring America’s Fighting Force,” directed Defense Department leaders to eliminate offices and initiatives related to diversity, equity, and inclusion. The directive followed President Donald Trump’s January 27 executive order of the same name. The Pentagon described the effort as part of a broader shift toward what the administration called merit-based standards and created a task force to assess implementation across the department. The memorandum put responsibility for carrying out the policy on senior department leaders. Its departmentwide scope made the review relevant to staffing, training, and programs beyond a single military branch or installation. The task force added a mechanism for reviewing progress on the changes, separating the initial policy announcement from the work of implementing it. The elimination directive did not itself provide a complete inventory of affected programs or measure consequences for discrimination, promotion, or unit cohesion. Those operational effects would depend on the decisions taken under the new policy.
